reason: The chapter's highest-scoring machine candidate and a genuinely tempting one, which is why it is written up rather than passed over. 'Governor over the land' occurs in exactly two KJV verses, Genesis 42:6 and Jeremiah 41:2, and Genesis 42:6 is Joseph in Egypt — the man who controls the grain, addressed by starving brethren who have come to him for food. Alma 60 is a demand for food addressed to the governor over the land. The resemblance is entirely in the situation and none of it is in the words: 'governor over the land' is the standing title of Pahoran's office throughout Alma 50-62, used dozens of times by a narrator who needed a title and had this one, and Alma 60:1 uses it in the flat administrative sense of a letter's address line. Nothing else in the epistle touches Genesis 42, and the direction of the Joseph story is exactly reversed — Joseph feeds the brethren who wronged him.

reason: Already declined twice in this book, at Alma 39:1 and Alma 41:1, and declined again here on the same ground: 'I have somewhat to say unto thee' is the King James Bible's polite formula for opening a difficult subject, it occurs in two verses (1 Kings 2:14 and Luke 7:40) which agree word for word, and the Book of Mormon has adopted it as Alma's own preface — 37:38, 41:1, 53:10, and here. Luke 7:40 remains apt in the way it was apt at 39:1, since Jesus says it to a Pharisee who is silently condemning, and Moroni says it 'by the way of condemnation'; but a formula used four times by one book is the book's, and no other Luke 7 material is present.

'Your blood be upon your own heads' is Acts 18:6, and the corpus has adjudicated that verse four times — 2 Nephi 9:44, Jacob 1:19, Jacob 2:2, Mosiah 2:28 — always for the same gesture, a leader shaking his garments clean of a people's blood. Alma 60:10's 'the blood of thousands shall come upon your heads for vengeance' has the head and the blood and none of the gesture, and it inverts the direction: in every Book of Mormon use of Acts 18:6 the speaker is clearing himself, whereas Moroni is charging someone else. 'Upon your heads' without 'own' is not Acts 18:6's phrase at all — the KJV's only verse for it is Ezekiel 24:23, about headgear. The verse does have a source, Acts 15:18, filed as a link on its second half. Registered so that a reader who recognizes the blood-on-the-head idiom is sent to the four places where it is actually adjudicated.

sharedText: enter into the rest of the Lord their God
reason: 'They do enter into the rest of the Lord their God' is the standing Book of Mormon formula, not a fresh borrowing. It occurs at Alma 12:36, 12:37, 13:16, 16:17, here, and Moroni 7:3; its mediation was settled at Jacob 1:7, where the KJV's Psalm 95 and the KJV's Hebrews 3-4 diverge and the corpus takes the epistle's form, and Alma 16:17 already carries a register entry to the same effect. What is new at 60:13 is only the application — Moroni uses the formula to argue that the righteous who fall in battle are not lost — and that is his argument, not Hebrews'.

Worth recording because the pairing is exact and the distance defeats it. Joshua 2:19 is the King James Bible's one verse that holds blood-upon-the-head and guiltlessness in a single sentence — 'his blood shall be upon his head, and we will be guiltless' — and it is precisely a compact about who bears the responsibility when protection is or is not extended to people inside a house, which is the whole subject of Moroni's epistle. Alma 60 has both halves: 'the blood of thousands shall come upon your heads' at 60:10 and 'will God look upon you as guiltless' at 60:23. But thirteen verses separate them, no other word of Joshua 2 is present, and 'guiltless' occurs in ten KJV verses while the blood-on-the-head idiom is the corpus's own by way of Acts 18:6. The compact is the adjudicator's construction from two ordinary phrases, and it is registered as such.

The machine ranked this on a five-word run and it looks better than it is, because Proverbs 10:3 is about food — 'The LORD will not suffer the soul of the righteous to famish' — and Alma 60:35 four verses later says 'God will not suffer that we should perish with hunger'. Two considerations sink it. 'Will not suffer' occurs in six KJV verses in six unrelated senses, so the run identifies nothing; and the word that would make Proverbs 10:3 decisive, 'famish', is a KJV singleton that Alma 60 does not use — the corpus's phrase for starving is Luke 15:17's, filed as a link at 60:9. Proverbs 10:3 is what a reader arrives at by working backwards from a theme; the wording arrives at Luke.
